segments.text: Please allow me to begin this session with a very brief question. If you were offered a job today, and that job could not guarantee you a reliable income, offered you no room for growth, and stripped you of your dignity, led to questioning your purpose, would you consider yourself employed? Or would you consider yourself empowered? But perhaps one of the biggest questions facing Africa today is not simply how we get young people into jobs, but how we ensure that they get jobs that allow them to live with dignity. So, we often measure success by employment statistics.

segments.speaker: Thabelo (Eswatini) · Moderator
segments.text: We look at how many young people are in the job market or the labor market. But behind every single statistic is a young person with an ambition, a family to support, a dream to pursue, and a future that they need to build. And some of their journeys are not straightforward.

segments.speaker: Thabelo (Eswatini) · Moderator
segments.text: Some will find opportunities through formal employment, others through entrepreneurship, vocational skills, digital platforms, and some even explore the informal economy. But regardless of the path that every young individual takes, the questions we need to ask ourselves is, are we creating opportunities that allow young people not to just survive in the working economy, but to thrive? So, ladies and gentlemen, my name is Thabelo Jamini, and I am joining you from the kingdom of SORD. Here under the wonderful support of YouthConnekt Rwanda and the SORD National Youth Council.

segments.speaker: Thabelo (Eswatini) · Moderator
segments.text: I am a television presenter, facilitator, and storyteller. I'm very passionate about conversations that challenge perspectives, connect people, and inspire meaningful change. So, in the next 90 minutes, I will be facilitating a conversation that allows us to explore the trajectories to dignified employment.

segments.speaker: Thabelo (Eswatini) · Moderator
segments.text: And it is my honor to be standing on this stage today as we navigate the journeys of young people and the barriers that they face in the work industry. First of all, just to start off our conversation, we will have a delivery, a keynote speech, from the Honorable George Obare-Addo, who is the Minister of Youth Development and Empowerment from the Republic of Ghana. As we know that YouthConnekt is a gathering of nations and allows us to share different perspectives from multiple nations across Africa and hopefully turning ours to solutions that we can use in our economy.

segments.speaker: Thabelo (Eswatini) · Moderator
segments.text: So, ladies and gentlemen, please help me welcome the Honorable Minister of Youth Development and Empowerment of the Republic of Ghana.

segments.speaker: Hon. George Opare Addo · Minister for Youth Development and Empowerment of Ghana (keynote)
segments.text: Hello! I believe the room is full with a lot of young people, but their energies are still reflected. Hello! Hello! Good morning, everyone.

segments.speaker: Hon. George Opare Addo · Minister for Youth Development and Empowerment of Ghana (keynote)
segments.text: Honorable Ministers who are here to support YouthConnekt from across the continent, our team from UNDP, established guests, development partners, young people of Africa, ladies and gentlemen. It is a great honor to deliver this address on this aspect that is central to African development and the future of our young people, trajectories of dignified employment. Across Africa, millions of young people enter the labor market every year.

segments.speaker: Hon. George Opare Addo · Minister for Youth Development and Empowerment of Ghana (keynote)
segments.text: They bring talents, ambition, creativity, and determination to contribute to the development of their countries. Yet, for many, the journey from education to employment remains uncertain. Too many young people are trapped, lonely, insecure, and unproductive.

segments.speaker: Hon. George Opare Addo · Minister for Youth Development and Empowerment of Ghana (keynote)
segments.text: This presents us with a fundamental question. How do we transform Africa's youthful population from a demographic promise into a productive force for economic transformation? Our answer must begin with a clear understanding that employment is not merely about having a job. It is about having work that provides a fair income, protects one's dignity, offers opportunities for growth, and enables people to build secure and meaningful lives.

segments.speaker: Hon. George Opare Addo · Minister for Youth Development and Empowerment of Ghana (keynote)
segments.text: Africa needs to chart a new trajectory. The future of dignified employment in Africa must be built on three important pillars. First, skills must lead to opportunity.

segments.speaker: Hon. George Opare Addo · Minister for Youth Development and Empowerment of Ghana (keynote)
segments.text: Our education and training systems must respond to the realities of our economies. We must invest in technical and vocational education, apprenticeship, digital skills, and work-based learning. In most African countries, our education is structured based on the colonial system that was left to us.

segments.speaker: Hon. George Opare Addo · Minister for Youth Development and Empowerment of Ghana (keynote)
segments.text: A lot of us go to school and get trained, not looking at what a job market requires from us, but what education institutions have built for us to train in. As we leave school, we are educated, but we have no skills to work with. In Ghana, our National Apprenticeship Programme is providing young people with practical skills whilst initiating such as the One Million Dollars Programme and preparing young people for opportunities in the digital economy.

segments.speaker: Hon. George Opare Addo · Minister for Youth Development and Empowerment of Ghana (keynote)
segments.text: Across Africa, we must ensure that young people leave our institutions not only with certificates, but with skills that are relevant in the demand for skills that can lead to decent and employable jobs. Second, enterprise must create wealth and employment. Governments cannot employ every young person.

segments.speaker: Hon. George Opare Addo · Minister for Youth Development and Empowerment of Ghana (keynote)
segments.text: We must therefore create an environment in which young people can build businesses, innovate, and create jobs for themselves. Ghana's Educational Programme reflects this approach by supporting young entrepreneurs to establish and grow businesses. Our entrepreneurship must support the assets of science, mentorship, markets, and technology.

segments.speaker: Hon. George Opare Addo · Minister for Youth Development and Empowerment of Ghana (keynote)
segments.text: We must move beyond encouraging young people to start businesses, to creating the conditions that allow these businesses to survive and expand. Yesterday, I had the opportunity of sitting in one of the sessions where young people in this auditorium advocated for support, not just support, but governments patronizing what they produce. I subscribe to that, and I believe that that is the way Africa should go.

segments.speaker: Hon. George Opare Addo · Minister for Youth Development and Empowerment of Ghana (keynote)
segments.text: Africa must begin to leave the past of government procurement to support young entrepreneurs so they can thrive. Third, an economy that creates productive wealth. Africa cannot achieve dignified employment without transforming the structures of our economies.

segments.speaker: Hon. George Opare Addo · Minister for Youth Development and Empowerment of Ghana (keynote)
segments.text: A lot of our economies are built on the colonial structures that were left to us, and so we spend more of our resources on our extractive economies. For instance, in my country, Ghana, we export more cocoa in its raw form than adding value to it. Honestly, we are changing that narrative.

segments.speaker: Hon. George Opare Addo · Minister for Youth Development and Empowerment of Ghana (keynote)
segments.text: Anytime we export raw materials out of Africa, we are creating jobs for other economies. If young people get dignified jobs, and if we are to change the trajectory of work, then we must add more value to our raw materials that we produce locally. It is the only way that we can create decent jobs for our people.

segments.speaker: Hon. George Opare Addo · Minister for Youth Development and Empowerment of Ghana (keynote)
segments.text: We must invest more in agriculture, agro-processing, manufacturing, tourism, the creative economy, and other competitive sectors of our economy. And once again, yesterday, in this auditorium, a question was posed. Which areas do young people feel that Africa should focus on in terms of work? And on the chat, I saw a lot of people talk about ICT technology.

segments.speaker: Hon. George Opare Addo · Minister for Youth Development and Empowerment of Ghana (keynote)
segments.text: I beg to differ. Agriculture has the potential of employing many more young people and giving them dignified jobs. A lot of our investments must go towards agriculture.

segments.speaker: Hon. George Opare Addo · Minister for Youth Development and Empowerment of Ghana (keynote)
segments.text: Back home in Ghana, we've launched a campaign called the Attractive Campaign. How can we make Africa attractive to young people? Where do I come from? We are positioned as a form of punishment. So for us in secondary school, if you commit an offence, instead of you being punished to do other jobs, the first thing they give you is a cut-flask and ask you to go and do it.

segments.speaker: Hon. George Opare Addo · Minister for Youth Development and Empowerment of Ghana (keynote)
segments.text: And so in the minds of many young people who go back home, agriculture was seen as a form of punishment. Africa has an ageing agricultural workforce. Most of our workers in our agricultural sector are ageing.

segments.speaker: Hon. George Opare Addo · Minister for Youth Development and Empowerment of Ghana (keynote)
segments.text: A lot of young people are not venturing into agriculture. We believe strongly that agriculture is what can lead Africa out. With all these technologies coming up with AI, what AI cannot do, AI cannot do food for you.

segments.speaker: Hon. George Opare Addo · Minister for Youth Development and Empowerment of Ghana (keynote)
segments.text: And so a human being every day will have to eat. And so once the demand is out there, what it certainly means is that agriculture can put all of us to work. And employment in the agricultural space is dignified.

segments.speaker: Hon. George Opare Addo · Minister for Youth Development and Empowerment of Ghana (keynote)
segments.text: It's one that has security across the board. And so I entreat African governments to focus more and encourage many more young people by venturing into agriculture. Let's make Africa attractive to our many young people.

segments.speaker: Hon. George Opare Addo · Minister for Youth Development and Empowerment of Ghana (keynote)
segments.text: We must invest in agriculture, agro-processing, and the whole value chain of agriculture. The African continental free trade area offers us an opportunity. We brought an opportunity to expand markets, strengthen regional value chains, and create employment across borders.

segments.speaker: Hon. George Opare Addo · Minister for Youth Development and Empowerment of Ghana (keynote)
segments.text: We must make African integration meaningful to the young entrepreneurs in Accra, the farmers in Kigali, the artisans in Accra, and the technology innovators in Nairobi. We must work beyond our borders. Distinguished guests, as we pursue this trajectory, we must also define how to measure success.

segments.speaker: Hon. George Opare Addo · Minister for Youth Development and Empowerment of Ghana (keynote)
segments.text: As it is not enough to count the number of jobs created, we must ask whether those jobs provide decent incomes, provide our young people with security, social protection, and opportunities for growth and advancement. We must pay particular attention to young women, persons with disabilities, and young people in disadvantaged communities. We must also recognize the importance of the informal sector, while quick-sustaining millions of African families.

segments.speaker: Hon. George Opare Addo · Minister for Youth Development and Empowerment of Ghana (keynote)
segments.text: Our task is to improve productivity, expand production, and create pathways for these businesses and workers to grow. In Ghana, we are strengthening the transition from school to work through our National Service Authority, expanding employment opportunities through our Youth Employment Agency, and exploring structured international labor pathways through our labor exchange program. This experience is a reminder of employment across the nation, across education, skills enterprise, industry, and labor markets.

segments.speaker: Hon. George Opare Addo · Minister for Youth Development and Empowerment of Ghana (keynote)
segments.text: No single ministry or program can deliver this transformation alone. Ladies and gentlemen, it is an important challenge before us as a continent, and so must our response be. Government must provide the right policies and enabling environments.

segments.speaker: Hon. George Opare Addo · Minister for Youth Development and Empowerment of Ghana (keynote)
segments.text: The private sector must invest and create opportunities. Development partners must support sustainable systems. And young people must be active participants in shaping the future of work.

segments.speaker: Hon. George Opare Addo · Minister for Youth Development and Empowerment of Ghana (keynote)
segments.text: We must also strengthen cooperation among African countries, share successful models, and create opportunities for our young people to work, trade, and build enterprises and growth bodies. The demographic dividend will not have to be automatized. It must be earned through deliberate investments, sound policies, and sustained political commitment.

segments.speaker: Hon. George Opare Addo · Minister for Youth Development and Empowerment of Ghana (keynote)
segments.text: Emphasis on political commitment. Africa has the people, the talents, and the resources to build a prosperous future. Our responsibility is well shown by the growth of our economies and states to dignify livelihoods for our young people.

segments.speaker: Hon. George Opare Addo · Minister for Youth Development and Empowerment of Ghana (keynote)
segments.text: Let us build an Africa where skills lead to opportunity, enterprise leads to wealth creation, and economic growth leads to decent work. Let us move beyond preparing young people for jobs that may not exist, and program-wide kind of jobs. Those jobs are no longer in existence.

segments.speaker: Hon. George Opare Addo · Minister for Youth Development and Empowerment of Ghana (keynote)
segments.text: In my country, we are targeting 300,000 young people every day. The public sector can only employ 5,000. So clearly, there is a gap of 295,000.

segments.speaker: Hon. George Opare Addo · Minister for Youth Development and Empowerment of Ghana (keynote)
segments.text: Clearly, the public sector can only have the leadership for that. And it is the same across Africa. We must give our young people the skills that we need, the jobs that are relevant, and help them awaken their mindsets through telling them about agriculture and other innovative areas where they can continue.

segments.speaker: Hon. George Opare Addo · Minister for Youth Development and Empowerment of Ghana (keynote)
segments.text: The true measure of Africa's progress will be whether every young person has the opportunity to work, contribute, and lead with dignity. Thank you.

segments.text: But I am a firm believer that education, good education, very well-structured education, can transform people's lives. And it did mine, and I know most of you here whose lives have been probably transformed by education. So here we are.

segments.speaker: Ms. Allen Kendunga · CEO, Talent Match
segments.text: We've all made it to the university. Our families, our friends, they are all looking up to us because we've made it. It may not be you, but the person next to you making it to the university was the goal.

segments.speaker: Ms. Allen Kendunga · CEO, Talent Match
segments.text: And here you are, you've made it. Everybody's looking up to you, and you're graduating, and everybody's expecting you to change their entire village. But you're stuck.

segments.speaker: Ms. Allen Kendunga · CEO, Talent Match
segments.text: You have no job, you have no skills, and everybody's expecting you to give back, to support them. My name is Alan Kenyatta-Seeds, and I run Talent March. At Talent March, we work with young people, specifically university students and research graduates.

segments.speaker: Ms. Allen Kendunga · CEO, Talent Match
segments.text: We prepare them and connect them to dignified employment opportunities. Thank you. When I started Talent March in 2019, I was only following a program that kept coming back every time.

segments.speaker: Ms. Allen Kendunga · CEO, Talent Match
segments.text: Oh, Rwanda doesn't have talented people. Rwanda doesn't have the right skills. You would have investors coming literally, and they would check all the boxes in RIT.

segments.speaker: Ms. Allen Kendunga · CEO, Talent Match
segments.text: And the one single factor that would turn back investors would be lack of skills. Talented, skilled people. And that would take away opportunities for a nation, just because we don't have skilled young people.

segments.speaker: Ms. Allen Kendunga · CEO, Talent Match
segments.text: So my question was, why is it that we don't have skilled people? What is it that we're doing wrong? Because every single year, we graduate thousands of students. So you can't tell me that there is no one in those thousands of students who can do a job, an entry-level job, a mid-senior level job. And something was broken in the system, in my program.

segments.speaker: Ms. Allen Kendunga · CEO, Talent Match
segments.text: And that's what led to the founding of Talent March. To explore ways you can support young people while they're still at university, to develop the right skills, to connect with the right people, the right employers. You know, some of us who go to the university, we have never even walked into an elevator.

segments.speaker: Ms. Allen Kendunga · CEO, Talent Match
segments.text: Well, you all of you are here, so you've made it. But there's someone out there who has never sat in this kind of auditorium, and the entire village is looking up to them. So we have two major programs to create opportunities for young people while they are still at university.

segments.speaker: Ms. Allen Kendunga · CEO, Talent Match
segments.text: And that specifically prepares university students to face their job market. When you graduate, you have to develop skills. And you will have employers and the private sector here, after my speech, talk about some of these skills.

segments.speaker: Ms. Allen Kendunga · CEO, Talent Match
segments.text: What are they doing? How are they hired? But you graduate, and you've never done a good job. So our work is to put you in front of the employer, to give you the skills before you graduate, parallel to education, parallel to academics, so that when you graduate, you actually have what the employers are looking for. The second program, because we realize now, like myself, not all of us are going to find jobs.

segments.speaker: Ms. Allen Kendunga · CEO, Talent Match
segments.text: Not all of us are going to have employment in the formal sector. The second program today, as I've mentioned before, and that focuses on supporting students to develop their professional skills, so they can actually start their own jobs, create their own jobs when they graduate, so that they should earn and employ more people. I have a team.

segments.speaker: Ms. Allen Kendunga · CEO, Talent Match
segments.text: If I hadn't started as much, I would be doing one job, and five, six more people would be sitting somewhere unemployed. Today, we are effective and growing. So we know that this works.

segments.speaker: Ms. Allen Kendunga · CEO, Talent Match
segments.text: Because I believe that Africa, Rwanda, we have the most talented people. I have seen it, I have traveled, and I know for a fact that Africa has the most talented people. What we lack is connections.

segments.speaker: Ms. Allen Kendunga · CEO, Talent Match
segments.text: And what we lack is equal access to opportunities. And that is where talent match comes in, and I'm sure that other people have heard similar words, but this is what it means. That given the right skills, the right connections, young people have, and the right resources, young people have the potential to transform themselves, their families, their communities, and their nation ultimately.

segments.speaker: Ms. Allen Kendunga · CEO, Talent Match
segments.text: So the question is not whether or not it works. The question is, why at least can this be reached, so that more people can grow, can prosper. So today, I'm not here to brag about what we do.

segments.speaker: Ms. Allen Kendunga · CEO, Talent Match
segments.text: What we do actually matters. That's why I'm here. I'm not here to brag.

segments.speaker: Ms. Allen Kendunga · CEO, Talent Match
segments.text: We trained over 1,000 young people, and of those 2,000, 1,100 of those are actually graduates. Some of them are in this room. I want to thank them.

segments.speaker: Ms. Allen Kendunga · CEO, Talent Match
segments.text: And of those that have graduated, 80%, this is more than 957 young people who have hotel employment, decent employment, within six months of graduation. Within six months of graduation. But what makes them different? I don't believe they also have degrees like other people who are sitting here who don't have jobs.

segments.speaker: Ms. Allen Kendunga · CEO, Talent Match
segments.text: They come from families not very different from those that don't have jobs come from. What they really appreciate about us is that they go through that entire path that transforms them to where they are today. So, I believe that each one of us in this room has the potential, given the right skills, the right network, and the right resources.

segments.speaker: Ms. Allen Kendunga · CEO, Talent Match
segments.text: We all have the potential. Thank you. And I want to invite us all, as we're seated here, I know that this room is full of young people, it's full of employers, it's full of development partners and partners, policemakers.

segments.speaker: Ms. Allen Kendunga · CEO, Talent Match
segments.text: I want to invite us all to take employment seriously, and especially our education. Education is the one equalizer, if I may say, for a lot of young people. If you have education, you can literally do anything because education should teach you how to think, how to solve a problem, how to find a solution.

segments.speaker: Ms. Allen Kendunga · CEO, Talent Match
segments.text: That is the purpose of education. Education is not about grades. It shouldn't be about your grades.

segments.speaker: Ms. Allen Kendunga · CEO, Talent Match
segments.text: Yes, grades matter, but so what after that? So, I want to challenge us all, educators especially in the room, let's rethink our education. Let's dive deep into our education and ask, is the education that we have created the outcomes that we need? And if not, what needs to change? And for policemakers and our partners, invest in initiatives that actually already work. We don't have to always start from scratch and build from zero.

segments.speaker: Ms. Allen Kendunga · CEO, Talent Match
segments.text: If something works, back it up. Scale it. Employers, I know some of them will come up here, open your doors.

segments.speaker: Ms. Allen Kendunga · CEO, Talent Match
segments.text: We want to learn. We have the hunger. Look at this food.

segments.speaker: Ms. Allen Kendunga · CEO, Talent Match
segments.text: People, young people actually have the hunger to learn, to take on opportunities. So open those doors, even if you don't have the experience. So, I want to challenge employers, especially employers, if you have never hired a director in your office, when you leave this company, go back and make a policeman say, 90 days from now, I want to have an intern that is structured, an intern that has a clear goal, they have work that they do, they get feedback, constructive feedback, not just a run because we run.

segments.speaker: Ms. Allen Kendunga · CEO, Talent Match
segments.text: So do printing work. And for young people who are in the room, and maybe those who have left my being in the corridors can hear this, let's own our own lives and outcomes. Our trajectories, all of these other people will help you, but you can only help yourself.

segments.speaker: Ms. Allen Kendunga · CEO, Talent Match
segments.text: So as much as you are calling on all the stakeholders to play their role, us young people have the biggest role, and that's taking ownership of our own trajectories. It doesn't matter how you ended up studying, it doesn't matter. Take ownership of what you're studying, and do something with it to explore other opportunities.

segments.speaker: Ms. Allen Kendunga · CEO, Talent Match
segments.text: So take control of your trajectories in your career. Get the skills. Find networks.

segments.speaker: Ms. Allen Kendunga · CEO, Talent Match
segments.text: Don't come to Africa Youth Summit, Connect Africa, Africa Connect Summit, and then you leave without one single contact. Right? The YouthConnekt Summit is a big platform already for youth networks, so leave with some contacts that you can actually learn from, leverage when you leave here. So let's own our own future, let's build the network, the skills, and let's dare.

segments.speaker: Ms. Allen Kendunga · CEO, Talent Match
segments.text: Let's have the audacity to actually ask, and to dare to want to do bigger things. With that, I thank you very much. Can we once again give a big round of applause?

segments.speaker: Thabelo (Eswatini) · Moderator
segments.text: Thank you so much, Ellen, for that delivery.

segments.speaker: Thabelo (Eswatini) · Moderator
segments.text: And what we're getting from that speech is that education needs to translate into real opportunities. And she's definitely challenging the entire ecosystem to be involved in giving young people opportunities and ensuring that young people are employable and skilled. Ladies and gentlemen, we continue to hear from the young voices that are in the room.

segments.speaker: Thabelo (Eswatini) · Moderator
segments.text: Please allow me to invite on stage the co-founder of umumbo.com.ng services limited from Nigeria, Adese Menutuki.

segments.speaker: Ms. Adaeze Menekpugi · Co-Founder, Omwugo
segments.text: Hello, everyone. Good afternoon.

segments.speaker: Ms. Adaeze Menekpugi · Co-Founder, Omwugo
segments.text: I'm super excited to be here today for the wonderful time of this trial right into my hands. So for a lot of people, their journey through entrepreneurship spans for very many reasons. For mine, it's a very personal one.

segments.speaker: Ms. Adaeze Menekpugi · Co-Founder, Omwugo
segments.text: In 2016, I had my first child. And like our culture is in Nigeria, either my mother or my mother-in-law was supposed to come take care of my baby at that time. But that wasn't my case.

segments.speaker: Ms. Adaeze Menekpugi · Co-Founder, Omwugo
segments.text: So I lost my mom at the age of 11. And my mother-in-law, a super sweet and loving soul, is your typical 21st century grandma who has a career, a business, and other things to tend to. So there's a mother who's supposed to be a sweet experience, but mine eventually became sad.

segments.speaker: Ms. Adaeze Menekpugi · Co-Founder, Omwugo
segments.text: As the people who came to take care of me, out of a place of love, I must say, but also lack of training and skills, made me do some things that actually endangered my health. My little baby actually had jaundice over two weeks, and nobody knew, because they didn't know what it was. But I remain grateful to God for that one person who came one evening.

segments.speaker: Ms. Adaeze Menekpugi · Co-Founder, Omwugo
segments.text: We managed to stop my son. She shouted, his eyes are yellow. I in fact, we all fell down and immediately ran to the hospital.

segments.speaker: Ms. Adaeze Menekpugi · Co-Founder, Omwugo
segments.text: Thankfully, we got there in time for my son to be treated, and there were no fatalities. This was what spurred me to begin Omugwa.com.ng. My name is Adeze Benepaki, and I am the co-founder of Omugwa.com.ng Services United, a social enterprise in Nigeria that trains and equips young women and youth with adult skills to provide professional postpartum care services for mothers and their infants. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Ms. Adaeze Menekpugi · Co-Founder, Omwugo
segments.text: Interestingly, I've come to realize that most young people, their first engagement with work-life is usually through the care economy, but sadly, without any skills, training, or exposure, hence the issues that we experience. Do you know that over 13.8 million Africans today are working in the care space, and a huge staggering number of these people have no form of training skills at all? And this is really huge, and we must surely do something about it. And that's where we come in, in our work.

segments.speaker: Ms. Adaeze Menekpugi · Co-Founder, Omwugo
segments.text: So you might ask, so how are you changing the trajectory? How are you formalizing the care spectrum in Nigeria? For us, first thing is training. Very key. People need to be equipped to the right skills and knowledge to actually do their jobs.

segments.speaker: Ms. Adaeze Menekpugi · Co-Founder, Omwugo
segments.text: Beyond training, I'm sure the young person in this room will be like, we've had a lot of training, so what next? Train and then stay at home? No. We go for that to engage. But before engagement, there's police vetting, background checks, medical checks.

segments.speaker: Ms. Adaeze Menekpugi · Co-Founder, Omwugo
segments.text: As we know, this space is really, really, how do I put it? It's critical and personal, because we allow people into our homes, so we need to be sure that we're getting credible hands into the homes of people. Beyond that, before the engagement really begins, the work engages, there's a proper interview session with the client and the caregiver. Some of them in person, some virtually, because we know the world has changed.

segments.speaker: Ms. Adaeze Menekpugi · Co-Founder, Omwugo
segments.text: We have busy families who can't always walk in to your room to do interviews. And if both parties eventually decide to work together, we have proper employment contracts that state hours of work, what exactly the caregiver will do in your home, number of days allotted for leave in the year, and even days for rest in the week, because they're humans as well. And with this, they feel really happy and dignified to go into the care space.

segments.speaker: Ms. Adaeze Menekpugi · Co-Founder, Omwugo
segments.text: And they are proud to go out there to say that, I work for Google.com.org. And the feedback remains the same whenever anyone walks through our doors. New people are different, and that's exactly what we want to do. And I believe that a lot of young people here can do the same.

segments.speaker: Ms. Adaeze Menekpugi · Co-Founder, Omwugo
segments.text: The care space is so huge, with a projected growth of over 3.4 billion US dollars. Sadly, we remain very much informalized and informal in this space in Africa. But we need to change the narrative.

segments.speaker: Ms. Adaeze Menekpugi · Co-Founder, Omwugo
segments.text: We need to provide the right skills. We need to provide the right training for people to actually do this work and do it well. Since inception in 2016, we've been able to train over 2,000 women and youth across Nigeria, and we've successfully placed 300 of them with families in need of professional care services.

segments.speaker: Ms. Adaeze Menekpugi · Co-Founder, Omwugo
segments.text: And for the rest, I'm happy to say that they've also ventured into entrepreneurship, doing their own thing. And wherever they go, I'm proud to say that those are our mobile ambassadors. All right, as we move on, I'd like to say that the care space is so huge, with a lot of opportunities to actually keep... All right, I'll just improvise.

segments.speaker: Ms. Adaeze Menekpugi · Co-Founder, Omwugo
segments.text: Thank you. So like I was saying, the care space is so huge, with a lot of opportunities, and the capacity to employ millions of young Africans and give them a sustainable source of livelihood. But we are still struggling with a perspective problem and a perception problem when we come to the care sector.

segments.speaker: Ms. Adaeze Menekpugi · Co-Founder, Omwugo
segments.text: I've noticed young people who don't want to go into the care space because they feel like they don't have what they could love more. Hence, the reason why we need to formalize this space. Because a lot of young Africans go abroad, and truly, that's what they do.

segments.speaker: Ms. Adaeze Menekpugi · Co-Founder, Omwugo
segments.text: Why? It's formalized. And they feel like it is real work. We need to do the same in Africa.

segments.speaker: Ms. Adaeze Menekpugi · Co-Founder, Omwugo
segments.text: As I begin to conclude, I'd like to state that for us, we've gone a step further to even start our own caregiving training institute, where anybody can walk in and get trained in different aspects of caregiving, such as postpartum care, care for the elderly, inpatient care, care for children with special needs. And we are currently working on our learning management system, whereby it will also avail more African youth in Rwanda, Kenya, and North Africa to still be skilled, and also benefit from this care economy. As I finally begin to wrap up, I know that we have different actors in this room, so I'm going to speak to every actor in the room.

segments.speaker: Ms. Adaeze Menekpugi · Co-Founder, Omwugo
segments.text: First, to our government officials and policymakers, there's a lot of work to do. This is a huge space that can actually reduce the number of unemployments drastically in Africa, if done properly. We need to set policies that will protect care workers in terms of remuneration, and also other benefits.

segments.speaker: Ms. Adaeze Menekpugi · Co-Founder, Omwugo
segments.text: We need to have inclusive social security systems that will actually cater for care workers. And I have heard various ministers and government officials say they have skilled trainees in their countries. Caregiving should be placed as one of those skills that could be done in these institutions.

segments.speaker: Ms. Adaeze Menekpugi · Co-Founder, Omwugo
segments.text: And then to our development partners in this room, you can do more good through caregiving. You can actually invest in the lives of young people through training. And this will also give them the opportunity to earn a decent, sustainable livelihood.

segments.speaker: Ms. Adaeze Menekpugi · Co-Founder, Omwugo
segments.text: And for the young people in the room, like I said, all this space is huge. And you get to decide how you want to feel in this space, either as entrepreneurs, or as skilled and trained workers that can actually earn a decent living through the care economy. For us in Only God Has Come, I want you to remain committed to creating sustainable livelihoods, changing the trajectory of that spectrum, and also creating dignified livelihoods for women and youths, not just in Nigeria, but across Africa.

segments.speaker: Ms. Adaeze Menekpugi · Co-Founder, Omwugo
segments.text: Thank you.

segments.speaker: Thabelo (Eswatini) · Moderator
segments.text: Thank you so much, ladies and gentlemen. And please give another round of applause to the true testament that some of our personal experiences can create opportunities.

segments.speaker: Thabelo (Eswatini) · Moderator
segments.text: And from that, we are getting that this big piece in the care economy, if you know, industry. So that is one industry that we as young Africans can explore and ensure that it is formalized in our different nations. Maybe we'll see more going into Eswantini, where I'm from, and all the other African nations present.

segments.text: Thank you. And representing our lead partner for this conversation, MasterCard Foundation, is the country director, Mr. Ivan Mwali. And lastly, please help me welcome on stage, Ms. Zora Kondo, who is the Chief HR and Development Officer for Rwanda Air.

segments.speaker: Thabelo (Eswatini) · Moderator
segments.text: Thank you so much, ladies and gentlemen, for all your patience as we went through this session. We have gotten into now a very more formal conversation. We've been looking at trajectories to dignify employment.

segments.speaker: Thabelo (Eswatini) · Moderator
segments.text: But this is a time where we get to define and highlight how the young people in the room actually get to earning a dignified sense of worth. What does it mean? Thank you.

segments.speaker: Mr. Ivan Ntwali · Country Director, Mastercard Foundation
segments.text: This is a question that actually young people have told us. Over the last seven years, we've been soliciting feedback in terms of what dignifying work means for them. And the one key critical piece is reliable income.

segments.speaker: Mr. Ivan Ntwali · Country Director, Mastercard Foundation
segments.text: Reliable income is quite pertinent for them. But other reliable income, young people want work that gives them beauty, they want work that's respectable, and they want work which is purposeful for them. So all in a nutshell, young people are looking for work that can allow them to thrive both personally and economically.
Technology is among one of the companies that are demonstrating Africa's talent, that it can compete on a global stage.

segments.speaker: Thabelo (Eswatini) · Moderator
segments.text: Thank you so much for that, Ivan. And now we look into how we can thrive as Africans in the global markets, particularly the Global Business Services, GBS.

segments.speaker: Thabelo (Eswatini) · Moderator
segments.text: So firstly, please allow me to get into helping us understand what scale of the GBS opportunities and why Africans are increasingly attracting attention as a talent destination. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Ms. Aileen Allkins · CEO, Teknowledge
segments.text: So yes, Global Business Services are generally companies outside of Africa looking to bring services delivered from Africa.

segments.speaker: Ms. Aileen Allkins · CEO, Teknowledge
segments.text: And the reason that Africa is such a great market for this sector is the sheer abundance of young talent. segments.speaker: Thabelo (Eswatini) · Moderator
segments.text: Thank you so much for that. And we're moving into Rwanda Air. As one of Africa's fastest-growing airlines, Rwanda Air offers a compelling example of how aviation creates jobs directly and stimulates wider economic opportunity through tourism, trade, logistics, and connectivity.

segments.speaker: Thabelo (Eswatini) · Moderator
segments.text: So Ms. Roy, please could you paint a picture of the aviation's economy contribution in Africa and its potential to create employment opportunities for young people. Thank you so much.

segments.speaker: Mrs. Dora Kondo · RwandAir
segments.text: So most of us underestimate aviation and the impact that it has on our economy.

segments.speaker: Mrs. Dora Kondo · RwandAir
segments.text: Aviation opens up, first of all, it connects markets, it connects economies, it links, it facilitates trade and industry, it links other sectors like agriculture, logistics, warehousing. So it is an ecosystem of many other businesses and enterprises that are connected to the aviation. So we should not look at aviation as just a means of getting from one end to another.

segments.speaker: Mrs. Dora Kondo · RwandAir
segments.text: We should look at it in terms of what opportunities are available in the aviation industry. Not just in the industry itself, but also in the ecosystem, in the industries that also are connected to aviation. And I'll give perspective.

segments.speaker: Mrs. Dora Kondo · RwandAir
segments.text: According to a recent report, in 2023, aviation supported almost 8 million jobs in the ecosystem and contributed about 80 billion US dollars to the Africa GDP. What does it mean for the young people? And they say, for every direct opportunity, direct employment in aviation, it creates another 22 opportunities in the ecosystem.

segments.speaker: Mrs. Dora Kondo · RwandAir
segments.text: That's how powerful aviation is. So my call, before I go to the question for the employer and the young people, let me talk about the new airport that is coming. segments.speaker: Mrs. Dora Kondo · RwandAir
segments.text: So what does that mean exactly? My call to the employer right now is we must move from being consumers of talent to being developers of talent. And the best time to have started preparing for these opportunities that are coming was yesterday, but the next best opportunity is now.

segments.speaker: Mrs. Dora Kondo · RwandAir
segments.text: So what are employers doing to prepare the young people to be ready to take these opportunities like I said, either directly from the aviation or from tourism, from hospitality, from warehousing, from cargo and on? What are we doing? But the young people also, this is the right time to position yourself and to see, no matter which field, you don't have to be an engineer, you don't have to be a pilot. No matter which field you are, you can position yourself to take advantage, but to prepare yourself for these positions that are coming. Thank you very much.

segments.speaker: Thabelo (Eswatini) · Moderator
segments.text: Thank you so much for that, Ms. Skora. Speaking of opportunity, one opportunity that is even more to most of us here is partnership. And Mr. Nani, the employment ecosystem involves governments, development partners, the private sector, educational institutions and the young people themselves.

segments.speaker: Thabelo (Eswatini) · Moderator
segments.text: Where do you now think that collaboration is falling short and what needs to change? Thank you.

segments.speaker: Mr. Ivan Ntwali · Country Director, Mastercard Foundation
segments.text: A lot of interventions are not sustainable when the work is silenced. Because when you look at the needs of young people, they are multifaceted.

segments.speaker: Mr. Ivan Ntwali · Country Director, Mastercard Foundation
segments.text: So it's very important that we have an integrated approach in terms of addressing the barriers that young people face in terms of accessibility and work. segments.speaker: Mr. Ivan Ntwali · Country Director, Mastercard Foundation
segments.text: It's a multitude of people. And I think somebody said something that was very profound. It's not just profanity, it's also equity.

segments.speaker: Mr. Ivan Ntwali · Country Director, Mastercard Foundation
segments.text: Because the needs vary. They're not the same. So the second one is the system.

segments.speaker: Mr. Ivan Ntwali · Country Director, Mastercard Foundation
segments.text: Sometimes there's a bit of a mismatch in terms of the education and the scheme versus the labour demands. Sometimes there's a discrepancy. segments.speaker: Mr. Ivan Ntwali · Country Director, Mastercard Foundation
segments.text: Otherwise, if we work in parallel, then we have the other challenge that Alain spoke to, of people who are struggling to transition into work. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Thabelo (Eswatini) · Moderator
segments.text: I think that deserves a big round of applause. And speaking of challenges, we're still exploring the challenges in different industries. Amy, please allow us to get into what some of the key constraints are that are holding the tech industry back and what could unlock its next phase of growth, especially from a continental aspect.

segments.speaker: Ms. Aileen Allkins · CEO, Teknowledge
segments.text: Thank you. We are an ITO organisation, but we provide services globally. We entered the market in Africa over nine years ago, initially in Nigeria, and then five years ago in Rwanda, both because of access to raw talent, but we were not able to find the people with the actual technical knowledge that we needed to hire.

segments.speaker: Ms. Aileen Allkins · CEO, Teknowledge
segments.text: So I think that's one of the challenges, to say how do we get people coming out of school and or university who have the raw talent, but employers such as ourselves have to have the willingness to train people on the specific technical skills that they need in their role. I think that also goes back to how to connect all the different partners in the ecosystem, because we were able to do that in Rwanda because of partnerships and collaboration. We could find the people, we have support for doing the pre-employment training to get them ready for the jobs that we needed to do.

segments.speaker: Ms. Aileen Allkins · CEO, Teknowledge
segments.text: So I think as long as you have people, which Africa surely does, with all the aids, adaptability, agility, and then creativity as well, so we'll put a C in there as well, but the creativity that are trainable, then I think technology is something that can definitely grow in terms of the GBS roles across the continent. Thank you so much.

segments.speaker: Thabelo (Eswatini) · Moderator
segments.text: And there's one thing that, Astoria, we need to explore, is that most times young people are seen as people that are not employable because they lack workplace readiness.

segments.speaker: Thabelo (Eswatini) · Moderator
segments.text: And you know, young people argue that they are not given the opportunity to gain that experience. And as an employer, where does that disconnect derive from? Thank you very much.

segments.speaker: Mrs. Dora Kondo · RwandAir
segments.text: I think the first disconnect is between our academic institutions, the graduates that are coming from the academic institutions, and what the workplace requires the graduate students to do or to become.

segments.speaker: Mrs. Dora Kondo · RwandAir
segments.text: So while academic knowledge is very important, it must translate to being ready for the workplace. And as I said, that's the first disconnect. We expect the graduates as they come to be ready for the workplace, and yet we have not prepared them, we have not prepared them for the workplace.

segments.speaker: Mrs. Dora Kondo · RwandAir
segments.text: That's the first disconnect. But still, a lot of employers are unrealistic about the expectations of what these graduates should come and do. They expect them to come ready with experience for work.

segments.speaker: Mrs. Dora Kondo · RwandAir
segments.text: So that's another disconnect that is there. But the third is the disconnect between how do we strengthen the bridge between the academic and the workplace. For us to ensure that we are bridging them, we have to make graduates ready for the workplace.

segments.speaker: Mrs. Dora Kondo · RwandAir
segments.text: So those are the three disconnects, but there are solutions for it. Again, my thoughts to the employer, we must create entry paths into the workplace. Do not expect ready graduates to come.

segments.speaker: Mrs. Dora Kondo · RwandAir
segments.text: We must create these entry pathways, and when we have these pathways, we must invest in mentorship, we must give opportunities for internship, for industrial and practical training. We must do that. But lastly, we must collaborate.

segments.speaker: Mrs. Dora Kondo · RwandAir
segments.text: We should not wait as employers. We should not wait for students to graduate before we can engage with them. The engagement needs to start when these graduates are still in the institutions.

segments.speaker: Mrs. Dora Kondo · RwandAir
segments.text: We participate in the career fairs. We prepare them. We give them academic internships.

segments.speaker: Mrs. Dora Kondo · RwandAir
segments.text: The conversations, the engagement must start before, so that by the time they are ready, they are already aware of what is expected, and they are ready at least to not come through the entry path that employers have created. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Thabelo (Eswatini) · Moderator
segments.text: Thank you so much.

segments.speaker: Thabelo (Eswatini) · Moderator
segments.text: And as we speak about transforming from the employment landscape for the young people, the young Africans in the room, what does a successful The Mastercard look like in the next five years, and how are you planning on transforming the employment landscape?

segments.speaker: Mr. Ivan Ntwali · Country Director, Mastercard Foundation
segments.text: We made a commitment in our Young Africa Works strategy that by 2030, we would like to support young people to access, dignify, and fulfill the work of a team of 30 million young Africans. For us, that is success. Applause If we can develop a world where young people have a clear path where they can convert opportunities and expect in them, that is success for us.

segments.speaker: Mr. Ivan Ntwali · Country Director, Mastercard Foundation
segments.text: And if, as an ecosystem player, we can facilitate all these different institutions to work in harmonious ways to make sure that we aggregate all the services that I spoke about so that we approach this problem collaboratively, I think that would be a huge success. That is sustainable, it brings everybody along, and it results into a long-sustaining impact for our young people.

segments.speaker: Thabelo (Eswatini) · Moderator
segments.text: Thank you so much for that.

segments.speaker: Thabelo (Eswatini) · Moderator
segments.text: Applause Stephanie, we're moving into a time where young Africans will not only survive, but they will surely thrive. I'll give one for the youth as well, if you don't mind.

I would say, first of all, start with the youth. When you have no work experience and you're talking to an employer, I think do take into account you have life experience and you have hobbies, you have volunteer interests. How can you package that as something that is applicable to work? So I have creativity, I can demonstrate my creativity.

I show that I can manage to type deadlines because I've worked on this project as a hobby or as a volunteer. Connect what you do outside to something that could be applicable to an employer. For policy makers, I think something to consider is helping, certainly, private sector to understand the benefits and advantages of hiring young people even without experience.

So how it benefits them to be able to adapt or train people to be adapting to their company, their environment, their policies and ways of working. But I think private sector needs to be encouraged and only government and policy makers can help them see with encouragement. And then I think the development plan is absolutely, as has just been said, how to bring all of this together in a cohesive way that can scale.
There are many, many hundreds of pockets of programs that are running but not connected. And I think it's that connection that really makes a huge impact.

segments.speaker: Thabelo (Eswatini) · Moderator
segments.text: Thank you so much.

segments.speaker: Thabelo (Eswatini) · Moderator
segments.text: And please give them a big round of applause. Thank you so much to our panelists for joining me on stage. Gratitude to the government of Kenya because as she was saying, she was challenged on the internship. That is what we need in Africa to give these young people exposure, to give these young people network.

It can only happen when you give us the chance, not only at the decision-making table, but also to exercise our skills and practice on what we would want to become in the future. Thank you so much. God bless.

segments.speaker: Thabelo (Eswatini) · Moderator
segments.text: Thank you. Ivan, can I please allow you to respond to that? Or should we start with Ms. Dora? Please, Ivan, can you respond to that?

segments.speaker: Mr. Ivan Ntwali · Country Director, Mastercard Foundation
segments.text: Thank you so much for that very good question. When we talk about criteria, the programs we run at the MasterCard Foundation are so many, and they are varied.

segments.speaker: Mr. Ivan Ntwali · Country Director, Mastercard Foundation
segments.text: So we have some programs, which are educational programs, like the Scholars Program, where people access scholarships. And I just wanted to flag that we work for partners, so we don't do direct implementation. So from the partner universities, each one has a criteria.

segments.speaker: Mr. Ivan Ntwali · Country Director, Mastercard Foundation
segments.text: But one thing that stands out, all those criteria are built around ensuring that the most vulnerable that you're talking about, that's our last mile, are the ones that are accessing the type of opportunities that we offer. segments.speaker: Mr. Ivan Ntwali · Country Director, Mastercard Foundation
segments.text: That's an example. And we have a lot of scholars, actually, that have been beaten in this room. So those are some of the young people, and a lot of them are from rural underprivileged communities.

segments.speaker: Mr. Ivan Ntwali · Country Director, Mastercard Foundation
segments.text: We have other programs which are related to entrepreneurial development. A lot of those have their own set of criteria, also through our partners. Some of them are organized in groups, where we do outreach.

segments.speaker: Mr. Ivan Ntwali · Country Director, Mastercard Foundation
segments.text: So outreach is done to last mile rural communities. The type of interaction that is with that has to be appropriate to the communities in which we are reaching out to.

segments.speaker: Thabelo (Eswatini) · Moderator
segments.text: Thank you for that, Ivan.

segments.speaker: Thabelo (Eswatini) · Moderator

Okay, thank you.
Bonjour à tous. Merci. Merci à Yurkanek, merci à Kigali, et surtout au Bwanda.

Cette opportunité, c'est ma première participation, et je suis très heureux. Je suis Francine. Tout à l'heure, on a eu une simulation avec l'histoire de la Minata, et le process précoce qui a conditionné son évolution et son insertion socio-professionnelle.

So, I would like to ask my question to my ex-husband. I am French, I was born prematurely, and it was a big shock for my family, for myself, and especially for this child who arrived. But something special happened.

This child was the beginning of my story and something very important. I liked the speech that talked about education because my parents were there. They told me, not to encourage you to do your job, but to tell you that you have to go forward.
So, obviously, I took a number. You have become a woman. And if you live, it's for you and first for these children.
So, I pushed, I continued, I said to myself, I give up. But my father, who was my pillar, decided. It was a second shock.

So, I say to myself, if I let my father go, it will be losing everything that has been given to me. I say this, why? Because I would like to say that Aminata was a fiction, but I am not a fiction. I am a reality.
I am an example of this kind of story. So, Francine, today, I am the one who set up the project, Generation Mice. I decided to impact my generation to allow Africa to benefit from its riches.

I observed in our environment. We have decided to move forward in Africa with industrialization, the creation of beautiful industries and especially new technologies. But what we have forgotten is to anticipate what could lead to certain consequences.
Example, those waters flowing by the industries of grassroots, territories using the same pollutants. Those waters are destroying us. They are sources of our cancer, lack of blood, and so on.

Then, on the other hand, I just look at our brothers, our grandfathers in the village. They were working on some crops like maize. And when they had already taken the fruits, they threw the maize stalks.
And those maize stalks were just born before the new crops. And when they born it, this was another source of pollution that could destroy our whole family. So, I decided to make the two things.
And now, I discovered that those maize stalks, I can transform them as a solution. I transform into powder and then into beads that are treating those waters. And we can use those beads four times.
More than the activated carbon that we are buying to most cost. The beads are low cost and we can use it first time. So, to work in that project, I'm working with the farmers in cooperative.

And I decided to train the cooperative in the first step of my project how to take the maize stalks, transform it, ground it, and then I can buy it and just transform it in the lab. That's the way I'm shaping my generational mission. So, today, my question is, if I choose this trajectory, can you tell me please, ladies and gentlemen, if this told me that I've decided to put it in front for my daughter, that I've made the caring, I want to know what is the commitment to help brave young mothers like me to move in towns of dignified jobs.
Because I've decided to take what was punishment at the beginning to make it dignity. Thank you. Thank you so much.
